skin.setting: a canal-side spice warehouse in Amsterdam, 1889
skin.title: The Scent of Bitter Nutmeg
skin.place: Van Dijk Spice Trading Warehouse along the Brouwersgracht, Amsterdam
skin.styleGuide: Moody oil painting with rich ochre, deep umber, and gaslight reflections over damp brickwork and burlap sacks.

rooms.name: the canal quay
rooms.description: An open stone embankment along the murky canal water, exposed to the cold autumn mist.

rooms.name: the receiving hall
rooms.description: A drafty timbered vestibule lined with iron scales and delivery registers.

rooms.name: the clove vault
rooms.description: A heavy brick chamber filled with the pungent, sweet stench of packed cloves, where the body was found.

rooms.name: the nutmeg loft
rooms.description: A dry, high-ceilinged storehouse stacked to the rafters with burlap sacks of nutmeg.

rooms.name: the pepper floor
rooms.description: A wide sorting room dusted with stinging black pepper dust where workers sift harvests.

rooms.name: the counting house
rooms.description: A cramped, stove-heated office partitioned with frosted glass and high oak desks.

rooms.name: the cinnamon cellar
rooms.description: A low, vaulted basement rich with the warm aroma of rolled cinnamon bark.

people.name: Willem Vos
people.bio: A weathered maritime agent who negotiates shipments from the East Indies. He has spent thirty years calculating weights and bribes along the Amsterdam docks.
people.voice: Blunt, raspy, and impatient, with a rough dockside cadence.
people.motive: The proprietor caught him skimming off-manifest spices and threatened to revoke his commercial license.
people.portrait: A heavy-set man in his fifties with weathered skin, muttonchop whiskers, broad shoulders, wearing a worn wool peacoat.

people.name: Hendrik Brandt
people.bio: A precise artisan whose palate determines the value of every blend shipped across Europe. He considers the warehouse his personal domain of craft.
people.voice: Quiet, fastidious, and formal, speaking with measured articulation.
people.motive: The proprietor planned to dilute his proprietary spice formulations with cheaper filler to cut costs.
people.portrait: A slender gentleman in his forties with neatly parted brown hair, wire-rimmed spectacles, and a pressed tweed waistcoat.

people.name: Anke de Groot
people.bio: A sharp-eyed woman who has managed the firm's ledgers through three decades of economic shifts. Nothing enters or leaves the canal gates without her knowledge.
people.voice: Crisp, concise, and bureaucratic, with a no-nonsense tone.
people.motive: The proprietor accused her of embezzling funds to cover family debts and promised police intervention.
people.portrait: A stern woman in her late fifties with silver hair pinned in a tight bun, high-collared black dress, and sharp dark eyes.

people.name: Bram van Leeuwen
people.bio: A physically imposing laborer who commands the warehouse loaders with a heavy hand. He has worked the docks since boyhood and harbors deep resentment toward the merchant class.
people.voice: Deep, booming, and defiant, speaking in plain Dutch dialect.
people.motive: The proprietor had docked half his crew's winter wages over damaged cargo and refused to negotiate.
people.portrait: A tall, broad-shouldered man in his thirties with a thick beard, rolled-up linen shirt sleeves, and a heavy brow.

people.name: Clara Vroom
people.bio: An ambitious heiress who bought into the company hoping to modernize its operations. She has clashed repeatedly with traditional management.
people.voice: Polished, poised, and assertive, tinged with aristocratic confidence.
people.motive: The proprietor refused to sell his majority stake to her family and blocked her expansion plans.
people.portrait: A woman in her late twenties with upswept auburn hair, an elegant tailored velvet travelling jacket, and an upright posture.

people.name: Pieter van Dijk
people.bio: The autocratic owner of the trading firm whose ruthless business practices earned him countless enemies. He spent his final hours inspecting shipments.
people.portrait: A stout, gray-haired man in his sixties with a furrowed brow, wearing a fur-trimmed merchant coat.

skin.briefing: On a damp November night in 1889, the pungent air of the Brouwersgracht was pierced by a cry of discovery. Pieter van Dijk, the tyrannical owner of the spice warehouse, was found dead in the clove vault, amidst overturned crates and fragrant aromatic dust. Five associates and workers were inside the compound during the fateful evening. One of them committed the murder and may lie to save their neck, while the innocent speak the plain truth.
skin.scene: A moody warehouse interior along an Amsterdam canal, gas lamps casting golden light across towering spice sacks, brick arches, and mist drifting through an open doorway.
skin.summingUp:
Look at how the gaslight catches the damp brickwork, casting umber shadows across the burlap sacks and the dark floorboards. The truth has settled into place. To begin with, the murder was not at six in the evening or midnight, because Card 4 narrows down when the murder happened. Hendrik Brandt is in the clear, because the killer and Pieter van Dijk were both in the clove vault when it happened. For that same reason, it was not Anke de Groot at eleven in the evening, because the killer and Pieter van Dijk were both in the clove vault when it happened.

Indeed, Anke de Groot, Bram van Leeuwen and Clara Vroom are in the clear, because there is no way for Willem Vos to have been innocent. Consider Clara's movements: Clara Vroom was not in the clove vault at eleven in the evening, because the murder had certainly happened by then, and from then on the clove vault held nobody but the body and the killer. Anke de Groot must have been in the pepper floor at eleven in the evening, because Card 9 has them together, and two people together are in one room. Likewise, Clara Vroom must have been in the pepper floor at eleven in the evening, because Card 9 has them together, and two people together are in one room.

Tracing her route back, Clara Vroom must have been in the clove vault at ten in the evening, because no door leads from there to where they were the hour after. That proves the murder was not at ten in the evening, because Clara Vroom can only have been in the clove vault then, and the one living soul in that room was the killer. Furthermore, the murder was not at seven in the evening, eight in the evening or nine in the evening, because Clara Vroom was in the clove vault, and after the murder nobody but the killer was.

Every timeline collapses down to a single convergence. It was Willem Vos who struck down Pieter van Dijk in the clove vault at eleven in the evening, after being caught skimming off-manifest spices and facing the loss of his commercial license.
